articles.title: South African anti-migrant protests: Cars torched and shops looted in Durban and Soweto
articles.summary: South Africa has experienced recurrent outbreaks of violence, often targeting migrants from neighbouring countries.
articles.body:
At least 24 vehicles have been set ablaze and foreign-owned shops looted in South Africa as anti-immigration protests descended into violence in two major cities, police say.

Unrest broke out on Thursday in Soweto, a sprawling township outside Johannesburg, the country's largest city, and Durban, a major port on the east coast.

The violence comes amid growing anger over a court ruling which would allow some migrants who had arrived in the country illegally to apply for asylum.

This had led to long queues outside immigration centres and the government on Friday said it would change the way it would comply with that ruling, without giving details.

The Department of Home Affairs said the current policy had seen its staff "overwhelmed", while "serious threats to public safety and order had emerged".

It said that the new policy would still abide by the Constitutional Court ruling.

South Africa has experienced repeated outbreaks of xenophobic violence, often targeting migrants from neighbouring countries.

'We have to prioritise South Africans': Anti-migrant movement blocks foreigners from healthcare

The uniformed group targeting foreigners in South Africa

Thursday's demonstration turned violent following allegations that a foreign national had assaulted one of the protesters in Durban.

Three foreign nationals were arrested in connection with the alleged assault, police said.

In Durban, in the eastern province of KwaZulu-Natal, protesters gathered outside a government refugee reception centre demanding that it stop accepting asylum applications.

Police fired rubber bullets to disperse crowds as businesses in the city centre shut their doors.

"There were clashes between foreign nationals in the area and South African nationals," senior local police officer Xolani Fihla told state broadcaster SABC.

"At the present moment, I can confirm that no injuries have been reported," he added.

Police said 14 vehicles were torched in Durban and 10 in Soweto, where gunshots were also reported during confrontations between residents and foreign shopkeepers.

Acting national police commissioner Lt Gen Puleng Dimpane condemned the destruction of property.

In Orlando West, a neighbourhood of Soweto, residents had initially gathered to demand the closure of small convenience stores, known locally as spaza shops, operated by foreign nationals.

Protesters forced foreign traders out of some areas, while shops were attacked and a building was set on fire, local media reported.

Police said reinforcements had been deployed to prevent further violence.

The authorities have promised to pursue those responsible for the destruction.

The latest unrest follows a July ruling by Constitutional Court, South Africa's highest court, which struck down restrictions preventing some people from seeking asylum because of how they entered the country or missed immigration deadlines.

The judgment means asylum seekers must be allowed to submit applications, even if they entered South Africa without the required documents.

This prompted hundreds of people to gather at refugee reception centres, fuelling anger among anti-immigration campaigners who fear the decision will encourage undocumented migration.

Government spokesman William Baloyi told Reuters news agency that people had deliberately spread false claims about the judgment, creating the impression that undocumented migrants would automatically be granted legal status.

Baloyi insisted that the ruling does not automatically give migrants refugee status or the right to remain permanently in South Africa.

Officials say applications will still be assessed individually and applicants will remain subject to immigration checks.

The protests forced tens of thousands of migrants to flee, with some returning home through repatriation programmes organised by their governments.

South Africa has struggled with xenophobic attacks for nearly two decades. In 2008, more than 60 people were killed and tens of thousands displaced during widespread attacks on foreign nationals.

The latest unrest comes against a backdrop of widespread poverty, deep inequality and unemployment affecting roughly a third of the workforce.

Migrants are frequently accused of taking jobs, contributing to crime and placing pressure on public services, although researchers say such sweeping claims are not supported by evidence.

Despite its economic difficulties, South Africa remains one of the continent's main destinations for migrants seeking employment, safety and better opportunities.

articles.title: Hoads Wood illegal waste "supersite" finally cleared at £15m cost
articles.summary: Concerns remain over the ancient Kent woodland's future after 39,500 tonnes of rubbish were cleared.
articles.body:
The clearance of a notorious illegal waste "supersite" in Kent has been completed after 15 months at a cost of £15m to the taxpayer.

The dump at Hoads Wood, near Ashford, which is on a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) known for rare plants and wildlife, was targeted by criminals who dumped nearly 40,000 tonnes of waste over six months in 2023.

It was the first supersite in England to have central government money spent on its clear-up, with work at two other sites bringing the total taxpayer's bill to £26m.

The government said the completion of works on Friday showed "just how serious" it was about tackling waste crime and restoring affected countryside.

The Environment Agency-led clean-up operation began in June 2025 and has seen 2,500 lorry loads of waste removed from the woods by specialist contractors to a landfill site in Essex.

The countryside charity CPRE Kent, residents and Kent Wildlife Trust joined forces in 2024 to campaign for the clearance of the waste, which was piled up to 15ft (4.6m) in places.

They welcomed the work's completion but some are concerned the criminal gangs may return to dump waste.

One of the organisers of the 'Rescue Hoads Wood' campaign said the cleared site would now be "catnip" to both organised gangs and opportunist fly-tippers.

He told the BBC: "Our biggest fear now is people are going to be able to access this site and start dumping on it again and unless the authorities are quick it will happen again."

The Environment Agency (EA) said it was extending the current restriction order in place that prohibits access and had dug ditches to make the site inaccessible to waste trucks.

Matthew Higginson, the EA's area environmental manager, said the regulator, police and local authorities had a joint "trigger plan" in place.

"That will bring all law enforcement partners to work together closely and much more quickly to stop anything like this happening in the future," he said.

Meanwhile, there remain conservation concerns over the future of the countryside site.

Ian Rickards, area manager for Kent Wildlife Trust, said it would take decades for ancient woodland species to return.

But he added: "It won't recover as it was but there are benefits to this. You've now got open space within the woodland. You've got wet bodies. You've got ponds. You've got these piles of dead wood as well.

"All of this will start creating, collecting and attracting wildlife back into here so it'll be fascinating to see how the site recovers."

The Hoads Wood illegal waste site is one of hundreds across England that include a number of so-called "supersites" - those that contain more than 20,000 tonnes of rubbish - that were exposed by the BBC earlier this year.

As well as the £15m spent on clearing Hoads Wood, another £6m has been spent on the clearance of an illegal supersite in Kidlington, Oxfordshire, and a further £4.8m of taxpayers' money has been allocated to the clear-up of a third site near Wigan.

In August, the government launched a national action plan to tackle waste crime, which it estimates costs the country more than £1bn every year.

But Hoads Wood campaigners have criticised the authorities for not acting quickly enough when the illegal tipping was first reported at the Kent site.

At the height of the activity in the summer of 2023, locals said there were as many as 20 to 30 trucks per day dumping waste at the ancient bluebell woodland.

The EA's Matthew Higginson said the agency did respond quickly to reports of the dumping but had to spend time investigating "to make sure we had a robust case to take to court in order to get a restriction order which closed the site".

Investigations into who was behind the dumping are ongoing, with three arrests made in February 2025.

Environment secretary Dame Angela Eagle said: "This government is taking action on the illegal waste sites that have blighted communities.

"Handing this ancient woodland back to local people, alongside our nationwide clean-up of waste sites, shows just how serious we are about restoring the places people love."

articles.title: New Ely museum honours two key World War Two RAF stations
articles.summary: The museum is based at a former World War Two airfield and includes a Lancaster bomber engine.
articles.body:
A museum has paid tribute to two former RAF stations that played vital roles in Bomber Command operations during World War Two.

The RAF Witchford and Mepal Museum has opened on Lancaster Way Business Park in Ely, Cambridgeshire, to show the contribution RAF Witchford and RAF Mepal made to the Lancaster bombers' offensive.

Grovemere Property bought RAF Witchford from the Ministry of Defence after the war and redeveloped the site.

"It really is just amazing that we are now home to all these wonderful items and can ensure that the experiences and sacrifices of those connected with the two airfields are remembered and understood by future generations," Thomas Brand, from the firm, said.

In 2024 the Brand family, which owns Grovemere Property, decided to create a new free purpose-built museum following the closure of the RAF Witchford Exhibition, which was located in the foyer of an office building on the business park.

Brand, a joint managing director of Grovemere Property whose grandfather bought the former RAF Witchford airfield, said the origins of the new museum could be traced to an excavation of a Lancaster bomber crash site at nearby Coveney in 1995.

"The project was supported by Grovemere Property, after local historian Barry Aldridge, who spent decades documenting RAF Witchford's history, got in touch," he said.

Aldridge, who died in 2016, had connections to the airfield that stretched back to childhood, when he explored its derelict buildings.

Artefacts recovered during the Coveney dig included a Lancaster engine, which later became a key exhibit in the previous RAF Witchford Exhibition, and is now the centrepiece at the new museum.

Brand said that many local people had donated items for the museum, which had given him "goosebump" moments.

"Recently a man gave me an old suitcase which contained his late father's RAF uniform, his medals, flight logs, flying helmet and a personal journal that documented his time in the RAF, it was incredible to see," he said.

Brand also said he had witnessed some emotional visitors who had found pictures of their loved ones displayed as part of the exhibit.

He did not disclose how much the museum cost to set-up, but said it was now being run as a charity "to help ensure its long-term future".

articles.title: 'Key evidence' in dad-of-two's death in Spain
articles.summary: Tobias White-Sansom, from Nottingham, was on a family holiday in Spain and died on a night out.
articles.body:
Four years after watching his brother die in his arms, Maximilian White believes new evidence could help him get answers.

Tobias White-Sansom, a father-of-two from Nottingham, died in a Spanish hospital in July 2022, five days after a night out in Magaluf, and his family believes the way security and police officers handled him that night led to his death.

A blood spatter report and a court order received by the family this month have reignited their hopes that criminal proceedings could commence in the Spanish courts.

White told the BBC: "I won't stop until we get justice for Toby."

The 46-year-old medical cannabis entrepreneur said he found it difficult to talk about the way he lost his younger sibling, who was on a family holiday at the time.

White-Sansom was pinned down at a nightclub following a row over him removing his T-shirt because he was too hot, his family said.

They told the BBC the Spanish Civil Guard - the Guardia Civil - was called and he was handcuffed, Tasered and injected with tranquilisers before going into cardiac arrest.

The family believe the blood spatter evidence - which forms part of an ongoing investigation that will see a court judge decide whether a criminal case is warranted - could suggest external force was used.

The report, which analysed White-Sansom's T-shirt, trainers and a sock, said several individual bloodstains were identified, which are compatible both with spatter stains caused through the application of an external force and with drip stains, produced by gravity.

An ambulance report, seen by the BBC, states White-Sansom had taken drugs and was agitated. He was administered a number of medications including fentanyl, the report added.

The Guardia Civil has not provided any further detail on the death.

At the time it issued a statement, saying: "Upon the arrival of the Guardia Civil police, this man was violent and police reduced him to be assisted by medical services.

"He was taken to the hospital for treatment. There, once while he was being assisted, he was arrested for a crime of injury."

Days later, White and the rest of the family were forced to make an agonising decision.

"The only thing keeping him alive was the life support machine," he recalled.

"And we discussed between our family members and we decided it was inhumane and we should let Toby die naturally.

"So then, my decision was to turn the machine off myself, and then my brother died in my arms.

"The doctors said he would slip away within five to six minutes, and Toby being the strong-willed person that he was, it took 11 minutes."

In the four years since, White said he had been trying to reach a resolution.

"The whole brutality of the situation caused my brother to pass," he said. "Someone needs to be accountable.

"It's accountability. And also, for his children to know that he was a good person, not a drunk tourist in Magaluf."

White said on the night in question, his teenage son wanted to go out but he did not want him to go by himself, so White-Sansom accompanied him along with his girlfriend.

"What never sat well with me was that my brother was not with a group of lads on a stag do," he said.

"It just didn't make sense. That's why I went so heavy in return, because I knew that's not how my brother lived and what he was about."

White spoke to the BBC days after receiving the evidence and a court order.

"The process is extremely gruesome because even when you're getting good news, it's bittersweet - my brother is still not here," he said.

"It's just the truth - fighting an uphill battle just to get the truth. At this point, it's a sweet picture but also bitter because Toby is not around."

An inquest into White-Sansom's death was also opened in the UK in 2022, and paused while investigations in Spain continued.

White believes the new evidence could significantly impact the process but if that fails, he says he will take the matter to the UK.

"The truth is out there, the evidence is there, we just need help putting it in front of the right people to get this justice for Toby that's needed," he said.

The family's lawyer in Spain told the BBC he had never seen a case like this before.

"I've never seen a case... with a whole package of circumstances and such a delay," said Jaime Campaner. "I've never seen it and I hope I never see it again."

He said he had been filing motion after motion to speed up the process, and said the Spanish Civil Guard - the Guardia Civil - was to blame for the delay.

The Guardia Civil told the BBC the case was before the court and it had no further comment to make.

"The Spanish investigation has been very slow," Campaner added. "And this is not common in a city like Palma, where investigations don't take so long."

He said the investigating judge in Spain would now consider the new evidence, and decide whether to proceed as a criminal case or shelve it.

"We believe this could be key evidence. We are not aware of the conclusions yet but it might end in results [for] this case," he said.

They are yet to be given a date for a court hearing but Campaner estimates the investigating stage would conclude by the end of the year, with a prospective court case starting next year.

"We all want to get this case closed and see some justice," said White.

"We're hoping that at some point in this chapter, we can close the door on this - and we can close the door on this pain."

articles.title: Dorchester justice museum staff sad to see doors close for good
articles.summary: Shire Hall has been opened in 2019 but the trust says it can no longer afford to keep it open.
articles.body:
The director of a museum has said that having staff furloughed and grants from the government during the Covid-19 pandemic hid some of its financial issues.

"It's a sad day for Shire Hall," said Virginia Smith who has worked at the museum in Dorchester, Dorset, from 2024 until it closed on Thursday.

The Grade I listed building was dedicated to the history of justice and home to the courtroom where the Tolpuddle Martyrs were tried in 1834 in what is widely regarded as a defining moment in the trade union movement.

The museum opened in May 2018 following a £2.9m revamp but its closure came after what trustee Rose Wallis said had been "several years of challenging economic conditions" .

Smith said the museum had been struggling from day one: "Some of the financial problems were masked by the 2020 Covid because the museum was able to apply for a lot of the government funding and the staff were furloughed, so those big costs were masked for the next two years."

Despite community backing for the museum, visitor numbers were down during the summer heatwave because "a lot of people would [rather] be going to the beach or just staying at home or trying to stay cool rather than visiting a museum," Smith said.

"However, I also think it's a combination of the financial crisis that is affecting the whole world.

"We didn't expect a war in Iran and all the consequences on the cost living that has come with that."

As a result, the museum's utility bills sky rocketed and Smith said staff costs became more expensive.

Thomas Hardy served as a magistrate at the Shire Hall, which opened in 1797 and was the county hall for Dorset.

It also served as the area's former Assize Court for more than 200 years until 1955 and the story of Martha Brown, who in 1856 was the last woman to be hanged in Dorset, has been featured.

Ines Lage, TUC Regional Secretary for the South West and a trustee of the museum board, said the decision to close was a difficult one to make: "The cost of living crisis has really bitten us.

"We've had stories of people sharing a pot of tea, whereas before they would have purchased two coffees.

"We have to sell tickets for people to come in, but obviously the numbers aren't coming in as much as we'd like."

Lage said the museum could no longer operate without having an impact on how the staff were paid: "Half of our operating cost is purely for the maintenance of this building and we are running with some fantastic members of staff but not as much as we'd like.

"We are supported by a wonderful plethora of volunteers and even then it has been a struggle."

Smith is now urging members of the public to visit other local museums: "When I started, it was a huge decline and funding became very challenging because we have more and more charities that are struggling and they are applying for funding.

"So the funders are having to really cut what they can offer. So, for instance if I applied for £20,000 I might have received £3,000 for a project."

Shire Hall Trust will hand back the keys to the building to Dorset Council in two months time.

articles.title: University of Bradford project to help firms 'adopt robotics'
articles.summary: The £3.67m Yorkshire Robotics Hub at the University of Bradford is hoping to bridge the "automation gap".
articles.body:
A West Yorkshire university has received funding for a multimillion-pound robotics project to help companies use the technology to expand their businesses.

The £3.67m Yorkshire Robotics Hub in Bradford is hoping to bridge the "automation gap", the city's university said, and has been partially funded by government body Innovate UK.

The University of Bradford said the programme would help businesses "adopt robotics and automation technologies", working with more than 300 manufacturers.

Professor Sherif El-Khamisy, the university's Pro-Vice-Chancellor for Research, Innovation and Global Engagement, said the project was not aiming to reduce human jobs.

"It will generate and create new jobs in fact, because the more we start adopting those robotics and automations in the production the more demand would be for the engineers and the experts," he said.

"Robotics doesn't mean that a robot that can bring you something in a restaurant or something like that.

"It is about enabling businesses to have automations embedded in their manufacturing pipeline to increase the efficiency of the production."

The project brings together the University of Bradford, West Yorkshire Manufacturing Services, the University of Huddersfield and Olympus Technologies.

According to the university, the UK currently operates about 104 robots per 10,000 manufacturing employees - well below the global average of 177.

The hub will operate across Yorkshire, it added, focused on the M62 and M1/A1 industrial corridors.

Professor El-Khamisy said the project would also benefit the university by allowing it to build relationships with local companies and improve knowledge and research.

"We have a civic responsibility to the community, society and the region," he said.

"It will allow the university to fulfil that civic mission more efficiently and more robustly by having direct access to local companies and upskilling the workforce."

articles.title: Deputy hopes Guernsey Airport roof fix will cost under £6m
articles.summary: Deputy Mark Helyar says the intended spend was cut "significantly" by reducing the scope of works.
articles.body:
Officials hope repairs to a storm-damaged airport roof will cost less than £6m, according to a senior deputy.

Deputy Mark Helyar, the States' Trading Supervisory Board president, said the original estimated cost of fixing Guernsey Airport's roof was about £20m but officials cut the intended spend "very significantly" by reducing the scope of works.

Scaffolding at the site was put up as a safety measure after the roof was damaged in high winds .

In a post on social media, Helyar said the States was unable to claim on insurance because the original company no longer existed and much of the damage was down to corrosion which was not covered.

The most recent damage happened in November 2023 when Storm Ciarán brought torrential rain and 70mph (112km/h) gusts to the island, dislodging several roof panels that fell on to the airside apron.

The States of Guernsey previously said the board asked the Policy and Resources Committee to agree to fund the project.

Helyar said the figure in the policy letter of more than £6m was a "high tide mark" and "not a price".

"Without the work, the scaffolding would have to remain permanently because bits of the roof continue to dislodge in high winds and are dangerous to the public and the very expensive aircraft parked at the airport.

"Without it the airport would likely have to be closed."

Helyar said the board was seeking approval to carry out "extensive structural repairs", which could take up to 18 months to complete.

He said the original contractor went into insolvent liquidation "many years ago", adding it could not be sued as it no longer existed.

"Buildings are only insured for loss caused by an event, in the case of the airport roof, much of the damage is due to deterioration of the fixings and corrosion," he said.

articles.title: Industry leaders discuss Jersey's high value residents scheme
articles.summary: More than 260 industry leaders met to discuss the role wealthy residents play in Jersey's economy.
articles.body:
More than 260 industry leaders from business, finance and law have held a meeting to discuss the role high value residents play in Jersey's economy.

Jersey's high value residency programme grants residential status to highly skilled and economically active high net worth individuals.

One attendee at the Chamber of Commerce lunch on Thursday, Mary O'Keeffe, said high value residents "were extremely important" to the island.

However, one former economic advisor to the government described the tax contribution of high value residents as "piffling".

About 260 families currently live in Jersey having relocated through the scheme.

O'Keeffe who runs Mary O'Keeffe relocation to help high value residents settle in the island said they contributed a lot to the economy and philanthropic causes.

"They are extremely important, so here today the room is full of private bankers, tax accountants, lawyers, people like myself and professionals who all work with high net individuals.

"So, they bring an enormous amount to the economy and that doesn't even touch on what they bring in regard to philanthropy."

High value residents pay a 20% tax rate on the first £1.25m of worldwide income .

They then pay a 1% on any income above £1.25m and there are some who feel these individuals should be paying more tax .

O'Keeffe said: "I can understand that but that's not looking at the argument the right way.

"First of all, the basic pay that they pay is £250,000 and that's before you even look at their worldwide income.

"And the 1% often equates to many millions and that's what people don't understand.

"High net worth individuals are extremely mobile, they are fluid, they can pick up and go wherever they want and they want to go somewhere that's safe, that's secure, that their wealth is going to be looked after and they're not going to feel that they're going to be ripped off."

Garry Bell, a tax advisor to high value residents, said if tax for wealthy individuals was increased he believed Jersey would lose them.

He said if the money they made above £1.25m was taxed at 20% instead of 1% it could damage the economy.

"If we tax those individuals at 20% the numbers would reduce dramatically. So instead of having a net increase of say 18 or19 individuals a year you're probably only looking at one or two," Bell said.

"So, we're sacrificing by seeking to tax them more, we're sacrificing that the direct income tax take, the stamp duty take, the employment, the GST, there's a whole raft of economic benefits that we sacrifice by actually seeking to tax those individuals at 20%.

"We are competing with a number of other jurisdictions, Dubai - zero tax. Monaco - zero tax.

"We're already one of the most expensive jurisdictions."

John Christensen, a former economic advisor to Jersey's government in the 1980s and 1990s was critical of the High Value Residents programme.

He said the amount of tax they pay is "piffling, frankly".

"I think it's quite divisive, particularly in such an unequal island community.

"As a development strategy, who benefits? They benefit because they're paying very little tax on their income but is it going to benefit young Jersey people? Not at all.

"I suspect its going to contribute more to ratcheting up of house prices, ratcheting up of prices in the shops, and a higher cost of living generally.

"And where they contribute to the island's economy, outside paying frankly minimal amounts of tax, lies with construction work.

"They've built endless, frankly, rather ugly and inappropriately sized houses."

articles.title: American billionaire Mark Cuban to Americans: You are getting the 'job killer' wrong, it is not AI; it is your rising ...
articles.summary: American billionaire and Shark Tank judge Mark Cuban has warned that rising healthcare costs, rather than artificial intelligence could pose a bigger
articles.body: American billionaire and Shark Tank judge Mark Cuban has warned that rising healthcare costs, rather than artificial intelligence could pose a bigger threat to jobs in the United States. The founder of Cost Plus Drugs said increasing employer healthcare expenses may lead to more layoffs and reduced hiring in the years ahead. In a post shared on social media platform X (forlmekry known as Twitter) Cuban wrote, “I hope people realize that for the foreseeable future, the cost of healthcare benefits will get more people fired, or not hired, than AI." The comments come at a time when fears around AI-driven job losses continue to dominate workplace discussions. However, Cuban argued that soaring healthcare expenses are placing a greater burden on employers, forcing businesses to rethink hiring plans and workforce costs.The cost picture of US health careAccording to a report by Fortune, the United States spends more on health care than any other country, and the total has climbed sharply. The most recent figures from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services show $5.3 trillion in spending in 2024, about 18% of GDP. That is more than double the $2.5 trillion spent in 2000. On a per-person basis, the U.S. spent $14,775 in 2024, nearly double the $7,860 spent in other high-income countries. Some studies find Americans use less care on average.Employers are feeling the squeeze. A Mercer survey of more than 1,800 employers found health care costs have risen every year for the past five years. Mercer estimates that cost per employee could rise 8.2% in 2027, the biggest jump since 2003. Nearly half of large U.S. employers, those with 500 or more employees, expect to change their medical plans next year, Mercer found. Common changes include higher deductibles or copays that raise workers' out-of-pocket costs.What the research saysPart of Cuban's claim has academic support. A 2024 paper from Yale's Tobin Center for Economic Policy found that a 1% rise in health care prices leads to a roughly 0.4% drop in payroll and employment at employers outside the health sector. "Rather than cutting wages, employers respond to increases in insurance premiums by cutting the number of workers they employ," the paper said. The study measures health care prices' effect on employment. It does not compare that effect with the effect of AI, which is the comparison Cuban made. Fortune did not cite research on that point.Why costs are risingFortune pointed to several causes: higher labor costs, new technology and pricier treatments such as GLP-1 medications. Some experts also cite structural problems in the U.S. health care system, including hospital consolidation and rising administrative costs.Mark Cuban's own stakeCuban is best known as a former Shark Tank investor and longtime Dallas Mavericks owner. He has become deeply involved in the health care industry since launching Cost Plus Drugs, an online discount pharmacy, in 2022.For the past four years, he has offered consumers a lower-cost route to prescription drugs. He says the company can charge less by bypassing pharmacy benefit managers. According to the nonprofit KFF, the three largest PBMs manage about 80% of prescription claims in the US. articles.title: Trump says US will not strike Iran before midterm elections
articles.summary: Oil prices drop as Trump dismisses speculation of pre-midterm military action against Iran.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has said the US will not attack Iran before the November 3 midterm elections.

The US president said late on Thursday: “we are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran,” in a post on Truth Social. “We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd.”

Oil prices fell early on Friday as Middle East supply concerns eased somewhat after tensions in the energy-rich Gulf region had mounted in recent weeks.

The possibility of renewed fighting had appeared to drive up oil prices in trading on Thursday. Some analysts believe Trump’s comments were an attempt to try and bring prices back down.

Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran is reviewing the US response to its seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and that Iran will respond within the “next few days”.

He added that negotiations are continuing through mediators, Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported.

Iranian media reported “massive explosions” in the southern Strait of Hormuz on Friday, with Fars citing unnamed military sources as saying tankers using “unauthorised” routes may have struck sea mines.

On Tuesday, US Vice President JD Vance said Iran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity as part of an agreement to end the war. Experts say this demand may signal a softening of Washington’s earlier insistence that Tehran abandon enrichment altogether.

On Monday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said negotiations with Washington were “futile”, accusing the US of using negotiations to attack Iran.

Russian President Vladimir Putin told Pezeshkian that Russia will “ do everything ” to help end the US-led war on Iran, Russian news agencies reported on Thursday.

articles.title: When is Navratri 2026? History, significance, facts, celebration, and all you need to know
articles.summary: We are almost walking down the streets at that time of the year when the evenings and nights smell of raat to rani, as the winter arch has almost taken
articles.body: We are almost walking down the streets at that time of the year when the evenings and nights smell of raat to rani, as the winter arch has almost taken shape; the dusk in autumn looks orange when the whole country seems to change its mood, and the streets fill with lights, markets crowd with people shopping for clothes, and the sound of drums and devotional songs drifts out of homes and community halls late into the evening. Even people who aren't religious feel it in the air.For many families, this season is about much more than a holiday. It is a time for fasting, prayer, catching up with relatives, and for dancing until your feet ache. Children hear the old stories again, grandparents pass on the generational rituals and habits they learned from their own elders, and neighbours who barely speak all year end up sharing food.Yet if you ask ten people about this festival, you may get ten slightly different answers. Some will talk about a goddess, some about a king, some about colours, some about fasting, and that is what makes the diversity of various cultures beautiful.But amid all this, confusion also comes up around the dates, when does the festival begin, and what day.To cater to all the confusion here, we have the details on dates and all that you may need to know.When is Navratri 2026? History, significance, facts, celebration, and all you need to knowWhen does Navratri 2026 start?Sharad Navratri begins on Sunday, 11 October 2026 with Ghatasthapana, when a sacred pot called a kalash is set up. It ends with Maha Navami on Monday, 19 October, and Vijayadashami or Dussehra follows on Tuesday, 20 October. The Pratipada tithi, which starts the festival, runs from 9:19 PM on 10 October to 9:30 PM on 11 October, according to Drik Panchang.What does the name mean?"Nava" means nine and "ratri" means night, so Navratri is "nine nights." There are traditionally four Navratris a year, but Sharad Navratri, in the month of Ashwin, is the biggest. There are other Gupta navratri also observed in the country, but Chaitra Navratri in spring and Sharad Navratri in autumn are the two most widely observed.Why is Navratri celebrated?The main idea behind the celebration of the festival is that good wins over evil. According to the legends there are multiple stories. According to one, Goddess Durga fights the demon Mahishasura and defeats him. Another tradition says Lord Rama worshipped Durga for nine nights before he defeated Ravana on Vijayadashami. In Bengal specifically, Durga Pujo marks the day of Vijayadashmi when Goddess Durga comes back to her father’s home after defeating the demon Mahishasura.The significance and celebration behind the nine days of NavratriThe celebration honours Durga as Shakti, the energy behind the universe. Over nine nights, devotees remember her nine forms, the Navadurga, from Shailaputri on day one to Siddhidatri on day nine. Many people also wear a colour for each day.In the north, people watch Ramlila, plays that retell the Ramayana. On Dussehra, giant effigies of Ravana are burned with fireworks along with brother Kumbhakaran and son Meghnad. In the western state of Gujarat, the nights are for garba and dandiya, and many people fast and pray together.While for Bengalis, Mahalaya, the last day of Pitru Paksha, marks the start of Devi Paksha and the countdown to the puja, this year it falls on 10 October in 2026, that is, the day before Navratri begins.For the Bengalis, main celebration is observed from Maha Shashthi on 17 October to Bijoya Dashami on 21 October; on Shashthi, the goddess is welcomed into homes and pandals. Families go pandal-hopping, share bhog (blessed food), and feed the needyGet the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: A 12-year-old Surrey girl handed her father £500 of savings and asked for a mushroom-shaped house; he built a two-storey backyard hideaway with a glass floor and trapdoor that went on to win Shed of the Year in 2017
articles.summary: A 12-year-old girl from Surrey, England, gave her father £500 from her savings and asked him to build a house shaped like a mushroom in their back garden.
articles.body: A 12-year-old girl from Surrey, England, gave her father £500 from her savings and asked him to build a house shaped like a mushroom in their back garden. Her father, Ben Swanborough, took up the challenge and built a two-storey wooden hideaway with a trapdoor, stained-glass windows and a glass floor overlooking a stream. The unusual structure later won the overall title in the 2017 Cuprinol Shed of the Year competition.The Mushroom Shed, also known as the Mushroom House, was selected from a record 2,963 entries in the tenth edition of the annual competition, as per the information on Shedblog. The event attracted 26,571 public votes, with the final winner announced by George Clarke during Channel 4's Amazing Spaces Shed of the Yearprogramme.What began as a request from Swanborough's daughter eventually became a place where the family could spend time together and entertain friends. The handmade structure included several unusual features, from a hidden shelf for treats to a glass roof that allowed visitors to look at the stars.Swanborough's creation first won the Cabin and Summerhouse category before competing against seven other category winners for the overall title. The judges ultimately chose the Mushroom Shed, recognising both its design and the effort Swanborough had put into building it for his daughter.A look inside the shedThe Mushroom Shed was designed to resemble a mushroom, with a narrow lower section forming the stem and a wider upper section representing its cap.The lower level contains a small desk area and steps leading to the upper floor. Visitors reach the top section through a trapdoor, which opens into a vintage-inspired living space.The upper floor includes stained-glass windows, a balcony and a glass floor through which visitors can look down towards the stream at the bottom of the garden. A glass roof also allows people inside to see the sky and stars. Another feature is a concealed shelf for treats.The 2017 competitionThe Mushroom Shed faced competition from seven other category winners, each offering a different approach to using a garden structure.Among them was Pricklebums, a converted summerhouse in Ludlow used to care for sick, injured and orphaned hedgehogs. Owned by Ailie Hill, the small structure could accommodate up to 22 hedgehogs during treatment and rehabilitation.Another contender was Team Unlimbited, a workshop in Swansea where Stephen Davies designed and produced 3D-printed artificial hands and arms for children free of charge.The finalists also included an underground bunker in Lincolnshire, a fire station-themed entertainment shed in Hampshire and a mobile 1940s police station display from Cambridgeshire.Despite the variety of entries, Swanborough's project stood out for its design and the personal story behind its construction.Andrew Wilcox, one of the judges explained why they selected it, saying, “The bar was set really high this year, from entire train carriages to a miniature chapel and a replica cinema. With strong contenders winning all eight category awards it was a really tough decision for me and my fellow judges. Ben’s dedication to his daughter and the quirky design details he created really stood out above the rest and he thoroughly deserves the title.”The winning prizeAs the overall winner, Swanborough received £1,000 from competition sponsor Cuprinol, along with £100 worth of Cuprinol products, a winner's plaque and a giant crown for the shed.Speaking after the announcement, Swanborough said the family had never expected their project to receive national recognition.“When we started the project we never could have dreamed we’d be here now. We’ve already made so many lovely memories in our shed, and now have so many more from the competition! There were so many innovative and amazing sheds in the running, and we’re absolutely thrilled to have been crowned Shed of the Year 2017.”Marianne Shillingford, Creative Director at Cuprinol, also praised the project and the idea behind it. “Ben has proved that you just need a little motivation and vision to create a truly stunning space at the bottom of your garden. His shed was definitely a worthy winner for the competition’s landmark year.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.standfirst: Raúl Varela, presentador de 'La Tribu', tercer invitado de 'Frecuencia Marca'
articles.summary: Raúl Varela, presentador de 'La Tribu', tercer invitado de 'Frecuencia Marca'
articles.body: Raúl Varela, presentador de 'La Tribu', visita 'Frecuencia Marca' para charlar sobre sus orígenes, su amor por el periodismo y sus objetivos con Radio Marca... que apuntan a seguir en lo más alto. PREGUNTA: ¿Cómo fueron sus inicios? RESPUESTA: Porque jugaba al baloncesto con mis amigos y queríamos tener un equipo mínimamente serio y organizado y el mecenas nos compró el equipo a cambio de que alguien fuese todos los martes a la radio, a la Cadena SER en Pontevedra, a hablar un poco del equipo y darle difusión al nombre comercial que tenía, que era Época, una tienda muy famosa en Pontevedra. Y fui yo el encargado de ir a la radio a hablar del equipo. P: ¿Y cómo recuerda esas primeras veces ante el micrófono? R: La verdad que, para lo tímido que soy yo personalmente, creo que hice un ejercicio de extroversión bastante grande. Ahora lo pienso y digo: soy bastante cortado y reservado para muchas cosas, pero en aquel momento no me importó. Eran intervenciones cortísimas, de un minuto pelado, pero a mí me parecían horas. P: ¿Recuerda algún momento especial de esos inicios, de ese ir poco a poco, que le enganchase y le enamorase de la radio? R: Pues el primer viaje que hice, que si no recuerdo mal fue un Baracaldo-Pontevedra. Recuerdo dormir en Miranda de Ebro, entrar en el viejo Lasesarre, que estaba pintada la puerta de amarillo y con el número 13 dibujado en rojo... Aquel año empecé a hacer muchos partidos, viajando por toda España. Me fue enganchando y metiendo en la burbuja de la radio. P: ¿Y en esa burbuja de la que habla, en qué momento y cómo llega a Radio Marca? R: Estuve en la SER bastantes años. Luego apareció un proyecto emergente que aún tiene vida en Galicia, como es Radio Voz, pero por cuestiones personales tenía que venirme a Madrid. Lo hice en septiembre de los 2000, primero a un proyecto de internet de fotografía y en cuanto surgió Radio Marca, que fue en febrero de 2001, tuve la oportunidad, a través de Paco García Caridad de entrar. Desde entonces... ya han pasado 25 años. P: ¿Recuerda ese primer día en Radio Marca? R: No, el primer día no, creo que el primer partido sí. Juraría que fue un Leganés-Levante para Radio Marca Valencia y luego un Liverpool-Barcelona por la tele. Debe ser que a Manolo Saucedo y a Moratalla les gustó, les caí bien y me dijeron: "Te vas a quedar aquí, ya solucionaremos el tema de tu contrato" y hasta hoy. P: De todos los partidos que ha narrado, ¿hay alguno que le ha marcado de forma especial? R: Entré en septiembre de 2001 y en mayo de 2002 ya pude hacer la final de la Champions, la novena del Madrid la del famoso gol de Zidane. Ese fue el primer gran partido de mi vida. Luego quedó vacante a la selección española en ese mismo Mundial y también me encargué. Y a partir de ahí, siete mundiales y entre medias, todas las Eurocopas. Aunque para mí, el partido más emotivo, el que lo cambió todo, fue el de cuartos de final de la Eurocopa de Austria contra Italia, el de la tanda de penaltis de Fábregas. P: Antes, el periodista tenía mucha más relación con los protagonistas, ¿recuerda alguna anécdota con ellos? R: Por ejemplo con Carlo Ancelotti, aunque es bastante reciente nuestra amistad. Mientras entrenaba al Madrid, un tertuliano de La Tribu era bastante ácido con él y yo empecé a defenderlo. Al tiempo, en una Supercopa de Arabia, me pidieron que me acercase a una sala, que Carlo quería verme. Me dio un abrazo, me quiso saludar y dar las gracias. Semanas después coincidimos en un viaje, juraría que en Liverpool, y se acercó y me dijo: "Te quiero invitar a cenar" y le di mi teléfono. Efectivamente cumplió y cenamos con nuestras mujeres. Fue una cena muy personal, muy íntima. A partir de ahí establecimos un vínculo muy bonito. P: ¿Alguna más? R: Sí, en un viaje con el Madrid el día en el que Mourinho cargó contra Pedro León. Había orden de que el avión tenía que estar en el aire a las 23:59, porque si no despegaba antes de las 12 no podía hacerlo. Había huelga de controladores en Francia. Recuerdo el poder majestuoso que tuvo el Real Madrid. Nos escoltó la policía, abrieron la valla del perímetro del aeropuerto, no pasamos ni siquiera por la terminal. Metieron los dos autobuses en la cabecera de la pista y ahí estaba el avión, el vuelo chárter esperando, con las escalerillas desplegadas. Subimos todos, tiramos un poco las maletas como pudimos y a las 23:59 estábamos en el aire. P: Últimamente el periodismo ha evolucionado mucho, se ha transformado, ¿cree que la radio ha cambiado o mantiene su esencia? R: Creo que la radio mantiene su esencia y que vivió su momento álgido en uno de los momentos de mayor desgracia que ha habido en este país, que fue el COVID. El esfuerzo que hizo Radio Marca, sin deporte, sin competición de ningún tipo, de estar al pie del cañón... fue emocionante. Ahora, por ejemplo, estamos muy volcados con los vídeos en redes sociales, con esa convivencia, que al final refuerza el producto y acaba confluyendo en la misma hucha. P: Antes usted ha hablado de La Tribu. ¿Cómo llega al proyecto? R: Yo he pasado en Radio Marca por todos los horarios. La Tribu surge porque la radio de repente pierde fuelle y se hicieron muchos intentos por reflotarla. Se estudió qué había pasado y se llegó a la conclusión de que éramos una marca amable, pero en cierto modo, una marca blanca. Apenas disponíamos de marca personal, no teníamos grandes personajes. A partir de ahí empezaron a cambiar las cosas. Yo empecé con La Tribu a la vuelta del Mundial de Rusia y hasta hoy. Los primeros años fueron duros pero entre todos hemos sido capaces de convertirlo en una especie de rutina. La gente se levanta, se ducha, se toma un café, se viste, se sube al coche y pone La Tribu. P: ¿Y qué espera Varela de su futuro profesional y de La Tribu? R: Que me suban el sueldo (se ríe). Me gustaría evolucionarlo, que la gente siga encontrando perfiles en los que se vea representado. No vamos de eruditos, de catedráticos, si hay que decir una palabrota se dice. Somos personas como muy cercanas y que, en definitiva, intentamos, a través del fútbol y la radio, ofrecer un cachito de vida a la gente que por la mañana madruga. ¿Su olor favorito? El limón. ¿El insulto que más usa? Matao. ¿Y la mentira? Escapo de ella, aunque a veces son necesarias para no hacer más daño con verdades incómodas. ¿Qué es lo que más vergüenza ajena le da? La mala educación. ¿Un miedo absurdo? Claustrofobia y bastante vértigo. ¿El contacto más famoso de su agenda? Nadal o Florentino, no los uso pero los tengo.

articles.title: A 16-year-old hiker used AI to plan a route in British Columbia and became stranded on a steep cliff; rescuers reached him by helicopter, raising fresh questions about relying on chatbots for trip planning
articles.summary: A 16-year-old boy in Canada had to be rescued by helicopter after becoming stranded on a steep mountain cliff during a hiking trip he had planned with the
articles.body: A 16-year-old boy in Canada had to be rescued by helicopter after becoming stranded on a steep mountain cliff during a hiking trip he had planned with the help of artificial intelligence. The teenager, Bryce Vincent Gowryluk, was hiking on Crown Mountain in British Columbia on Saturday, when he lost his way and ended up on a dangerous climbing route.According to People magazine, the teenager had used Claude AI, an artificial intelligence assistant developed by Anthropic, to help plan his hike. However, he eventually moved away from the usual hiking trail and reached a section of the mountain where he could neither safely continue nor return.The situation became serious when he found himself trapped on a narrow ledge along an almost vertical cliff. He contacted the police for help, following which North Shore Rescue was called to the mountain. The rescue operation required a helicopter and specialised climbing equipment because the location was difficult to reach.The teenager was eventually brought to safety after spending several hours stranded on the mountain. The incident has also prompted rescuers to warn hikers against relying entirely on AI-generated routes when planning trips through difficult mountain terrain.What happened during the hikeAccording to North Shore News, the teenager began his hike from Grouse Mountain and intended to reach Crown Mountain. Paul Markey, search manager for North Shore Rescue, said the planned hike was difficult and normally took around seven to eight hours to complete.Markey said the boy had used Claude AI while preparing for the trip. According to him, the AI assistant suggested a particularly challenging route that eventually led to the teenager becoming stranded.North Shore Rescue later explained that the hiker had moved far away from the established Crown Mountain hiking route. However, rescuers were unable to determine exactly where or how he had taken the wrong turn.“It turns out that this hiker had somehow got far off the Crown hiking route and became stranded on a climbing route known as the ‘Widowmaker’, at the base of its final headwall,” the rescue organisation wrote.Speaking to The New York Times, Bryce acknowledged that he had mistakenly entered an area known as Widowmaker Arete. He said he did not blame the AI assistant entirely because he had also used Google Maps and other tools while planning his journey.The teenager explained that he continued walking because he believed he was in a different location. By the time the route became “too sketchy”, he realised he was “trapped on a ledge” on an almost vertical cliff. Markey told also CTV News that a fall from the location could have caused serious injuries or even death.The difficult rescueNorth Shore Rescue received information about the stranded teenager at approximately 3.30 pm on Saturday. By then, he was stuck in an area that was difficult for rescue teams to approach.A helicopter was deployed to reach the mountain, but the aircraft could not land directly beside the teenager because of the steep terrain.Therefore, rescue technicians had to land at a higher location and descend towards him using ropes. Once a rescuer reached the teenager, additional safety equipment was secured to help move him away from the dangerous section of the cliff.“There, the member established additional protection and was able to move the subject to a suitable extraction point,” North Shore Rescue said in its account of the operation.After the teenager was moved to a safer position, he was lifted into the rescue helicopter. The aircraft then transported him to a rescue base near Cleveland Dam. The operation took approximately three hours from the time rescuers received the initial call.“The boy was very scared. He definitely feared for his life,” Markey told North Shore News.Mother recalls son's distressDuring the incident, Bryce managed to contact the police, who alerted North Shore Rescue. He also called his mother, Joelle, while waiting for help.Speaking to The New York Times, Joelle said her son had started the hike with good intentions but had ended up in a frightening situation.“He had very good intentions going in, but it’s never the call that a parent wants- that he needs a helicopter rescue,” she said.Rescuers warn against AI Following the rescue, Markey warned that hikers should not depend entirely on artificial intelligence when choosing routes through mountainous areas.He said AI assistants do not have first-hand experience of the terrain and cannot replace proper knowledge of the area, navigation skills and training.“Claude has never been in that specific area, has never been on that route, and has never been in the outdoors. Do your own research and gain your own knowledge of the area and supplement it with training and navigation,” Markey told CTV News.This is not first such incident, however. Most recently, three rookie Roseville hikers were stranded during their climb of Mount Shasta, last month. They heavily relied on Google Gemini for their trip. Similarly, in August 2023, a student nurse was stranded in the Central Australian Dessert withiut food and water after following Google Maps.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Heavy rain batters Chile’s capital, sweeping away cars and flooding homes
articles.summary: Heavy rains drenched Chile’s capital and the surrounding region, triggering mudslides that swept cars through streets, flooded homes, forced residents to evacuate and injured at least six people, authorities said.
articles.body: SANTIAGO, Chile — Heavy rains drenched Chile’s capital and the surrounding region Thursday, triggering mudslides that swept cars through streets, flooded homes, forced residents to evacuate and injured at least six people, authorities said. President José Antonio Kast declared a state of emergency for Las Condes, a wealthy suburb east of Santiago, giving government agencies more power to respond as torrential rains turned key roads into impassable waterways. The district’s mayor, Catalina San Martín, said 14.4 centimeters (5.7 inches) of rain had fallen in recent days — about nine times the average October rainfall — leaving the area “totally saturated.” The Mapocho River, which runs through Santiago, overflowed, prompting evacuation orders. Chile’s disaster-response agency put 10 other districts on high alert for more landslides and ordered schools to close Friday. Rain storms earlier this week had already damaged a few dozen homes across central Chile and left nearly 12,000 customers in Santiago without power, officials said. The downpours were expected to ease Friday. No deaths were reported Thursday. The injured included a 1-year-old child with broken bones, officials said. Firefighters said they’d rescued or evacuated more than 1,000 people. The floods come as a powerful El Niño gains strength. The naturally recurring warming of tropical Pacific waters scrambles rainfall patterns worldwide and often brings wetter springs to the Southern Hemisphere. The World Meteorological Organization said Thursday that this year’s El Niño was expected to peak in December and could be among the most intense since at least 1950.

articles.title: 'Unwarranted, offensive': India slams US Vice President JD Vance 'indentured servants' amid H-1B visa row
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Friday slammed US vice-president JD Vance over his description of H-1B visa workers as \"indentured
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Friday slammed US vice-president JD Vance over his description of H-1B visa workers as "indentured servants", calling his remarks "unwarranted" and "deeply offensive".In a statement, responding to Vance’s comments, the ministry said, "We have also seen some comments in this context by the US Vice President. We believe that such descriptions are unwarranted and ignore the fact that Indian professionals in the United States are highly educated and skilled contributors to its economy and innovation ecosystem."The MEA also highlighted the contribution of immigrants to the US economy, saying, "Indeed, the history of the United States itself has been shaped by generations of immigrants whose labour, enterprise and innovation have contributed to its growth and prosperity.""Resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive," it added.Vance made the remarks while addressing a news conference on visa fraud, alleging that companies bring in foreign workers at lower wages while laying off American employees.“If you are working as an H-1B visa in the United States of America, you’re earning $20,000 less than an American citizen hired in the same position. If you were brought in by one of these foreign outsourcing firms, you’re making $48,000 less than an American citizen in a similar position," Vance said."So, I’m sure that everybody here understands the game that is being played. You bring in indentured servants from outside the country, you lay off American workers and, if you’re a corporation, you make a ton of money by under cutting the wages of American workers, replacing them with people who frankly shouldn’t be in the United States of America to begin with,” he added.The MEA said that it was aware of the US department of labor’s decision concerning the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) programme for certain companies."It should also be clear that talent mobility adds value to both economies. While it creates opportunities for Indians, it equally helps US companies with cutting-edge talent, innovation, research, productivity, competitiveness and job creation, besides creating shareholder wealth in the US," the statement said."This is therefore an area of tremendous mutual benefit for the two countries and our expectation is that all stakeholders in this process can appreciate this fact. The steps announced by the US do not advance the shared ambitions of both countries,” it added.The MEA also clarified that PERM is separate from the H-1B visa programme. It said the suspension of PERM applications does not, by itself, affect the validity of existing H-1B visas or the status of visa holders and their dependents, although it could affect the green card process for eligible employees of the companies concerned.“We continue to follow developments around this issue,” the ministry added.The MEA’s response came a day after the Trump administration suspended eight companies, TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech, Cognizant, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe, from participating in the PERM programme.The US administration’s move is part of a broader crackdown on skilled-worker immigration. US officials have alleged that companies have used the system at the expense of American workers.The US department of labor said it would stop accepting and processing new and pending PERM applications involving the affected companies.PERM is an important step in the employment-based green card process. Employers generally need labour certification from the US department of labor before sponsoring eligible foreign workers for permanent residence.The process requires employers to establish that there are not enough qualified, willing and available US workers for a position and that hiring a foreign worker will not adversely affect wages and working conditions.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Kashmiri filmmaker Arfat Sheikh released from U.S. ICE detention, campaign says
articles.summary: Award-winning Kashmiri filmmaker Arfat Sheikh was released from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention on bond Thursday after being detained on Sept. 24, according to a statement by a campaign of his friends and relatives to free him.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Award-winning Kashmiri filmmaker Arfat Sheikh was released from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention on bond Thursday after being detained on Sept. 24, according to a statement by a campaign of his friends and relatives to free him. Sheikh, whose work has ​explored conflict in his native India-administered Kashmir, was detained by ICE, part of the Department of Homeland Security, while coming off ​a plane from California at Washington Dulles International Airport, the campaign said. It said Sheikh’s bond was granted Tuesday and he was released on Thursday, adding that the deportation case against him continues. The campaign said Sheikh, who lived in Alexandria, Virginia, entered the United States in 2019 on a student visa to pursue graduate studies in film at Georgia State University and filed for asylum in 2020. The campaign said he had a ​pending immigration application and was authorized to work and live in the U.S. DHS said Wednesday that Sheikh was arrested on Sept. 24. It said ​Sheikh “legally entered the U.S. on a temporary basis and illegally overstayed his lawful admittance.” A pending ​application does not confer legal status in the U.S., DHS said, adding that he ⁠will receive due process. President Donald Trump’s administration said in August that it was ‌working “to identify ⁠and revoke the non-immigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the U.S. claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently.” Trump has pursued an immigration crackdown and deportation drive that he says aims to improve domestic security. Rights advocates say the crackdown has violated due process and ​free speech rights and created an unsafe ⁠environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling. Sheikh’s first feature film, 2024’s “Saffron Kingdom,” won Best Feature Film at the Chicago Filmmakers Awards, ​the LA Film and Documentary Awards, the Melbourne Independent Film Festival and the ​Wake Forest ⁠Film Festival. Sheikh won the Emerging Filmmaker Activist Award at the Teaneck International Film Festival. The film explored conflict in Kashmir through the journey of a family from Srinagar in India-administered Kashmir ⁠in ​the 1990s to Atlanta in 2019. Muslim-majority Kashmir is claimed in full ​by both Hindu-majority India and Muslim-majority Pakistan, but each control only part of it and have fought wars over the territory. India revoked ​Kashmir’s constitutional autonomy in August 2019.

articles.title: Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navanethem ‘Navi’ Pillay for her efforts to promote international law
articles.summary: Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay
articles.body: The Nobel Peace Prize was awarded Friday to the South African jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law. Other frontrunners had included Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of anti-Kremlin figure Alexei Navalny, Ugandan climate activist Vanessa Nakate, Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms, and Mykola Kuleba, who founded an organization to rescue Ukrainian children abducted and forcibly deported by Russia. President Donald Trump was among the 287 candidates, according to the leaders of Israel, Pakistan and Cambodia, which said they nominated him. But despite long coveting the award, President Donald Trump said this week he didn’t think he would win. “I don’t know what their decision is going to be,” Trump said in the Oval Office. “They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me.” Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado gave her 2025 Nobel Peace Prize medal to Trump in January as she sought U.S. support for her efforts in Venezuela.
